intro: After the five books of the Torah, the Bible tells a long story in order. A people crosses a river into a land. Leaders rise up when there is trouble. Then the people ask for a king. This unit follows that story through the books of Joshua, Judges, Ruth, Samuel and the first part of Kings. Jewish readers call most of these books the Former Prophets. Christian readers call them the Historical Books.

You will meet Joshua at Jericho and Deborah under her palm tree. You will meet Gideon with three hundred men and Samson with his uncut hair. You will walk with Ruth from Moab to Bethlehem. You will watch Samuel anoint Saul and then David. You will see David face a giant, become a king and make a terrible mistake. You will hear Solomon judge two mothers and build a Temple. Then you will see his kingdom split in two.

Along the way you will learn what a judge was and what a covenant is. You will learn what the text says a king was supposed to do. You will read short passages from the King James Version and put them in your own words. And you will practice a skill that matters for the whole course. Say what a story says. Say how its readers have read it. Do not decide for anyone what to believe.
bigQuestion: What do the stories of the judges and the first kings show about what their readers valued in a leader?

timeline.t: The book of Joshua sets the crossing of the Jordan and the fall of Jericho around this time, as many scholars date the story
The period of the judges begins: Deborah, Gideon, Samson and others, as the book of Judges tells it
The book of Ruth is set in the days of the judges, in Bethlehem and Moab
Samuel anoints Saul, the first king, according to 1 Samuel
David becomes king and makes Jerusalem his capital
Solomon builds the First Temple in Jerusalem, as 1 Kings describes
The kingdom splits into Israel in the north and Judah in the south
Assyria conquers the northern kingdom of Israel
Babylon captures Jerusalem and destroys the First Temple
The King James Version, which this unit quotes, is printed in England
The Jewish Publication Society prints its English Tanakh

words.d: the Jewish name for Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings
the Christian name for Joshua through Esther, which tell a story in order
a very large family group with its own name; the Bible counts twelve tribes of Israel
a binding promise with rules on both sides; in the Hebrew Bible, the bond between God and Israel
in the book of Judges, a leader who rises up to rescue the people in a time of trouble
a person who speaks a message from God, such as Deborah, Samuel or Nathan
a Hebrew word for loyal kindness that goes beyond what is required; the main idea of Ruth
gathering leftover grain after the harvest, which the Torah says must be left for the poor and the stranger
to pour oil on a person's head as a sign that they are chosen for a job, such as king
a short story that teaches by making the listener see something in a new way
the house of worship Solomon built in Jerusalem, where the priests served and the ark was kept
after the split, the southern kingdom with Jerusalem and the Temple

test.q: Which book comes first in this unit's story?
test.why: Joshua follows Deuteronomy and tells of crossing the Jordan. Judges, Ruth and Samuel come after.

test.q: What does the word judge mean in the book of Judges?
choices: A leader who rises up in a crisis
A person who copies the law
test.why: Judges are rescuers raised up in trouble, such as Deborah and Gideon, not courtroom officials.

test.q: What does the last verse of Judges say?
choices: There was no king, and everyone did what was right in their own eyes
test.why: Judges 21:25 closes the book with this line. Many readers see it as a hint that a king is coming.

test.q: Who said, Where you go, I will go?
test.why: Ruth 1:16 gives Ruth's promise to her mother-in-law Naomi on the road to Bethlehem.

test.q: Which tribe held no land of its own and served at the place of worship?
test.why: Joshua 21 says the Levites lived in towns spread among the other tribes.

test.q: Who was the mother who prayed at Shiloh for a son?
test.why: 1 Samuel 1 tells of Hannah's prayer. Her son was Samuel.

test.q: What did Samuel warn a king would do?
choices: Take sons, daughters, fields and a tenth of the grain
test.why: 1 Samuel 8 lists what a king will take from the people. They asked for a king anyway.

test.q: What did David use against Goliath?
test.why: 1 Samuel 17 says David took off Saul's armor and went out with a sling and five smooth stones.

test.q: Who was David's closest friend, the son of King Saul?
test.why: Jonathan protected David from his father's jealousy. Nathan was a prophet and Boaz married Ruth.

test.q: What did David do at Jerusalem after he captured it?
choices: He brought the ark there and made it his capital
He gave it to the Philistines
test.why: 2 Samuel 5 and 6 tell how David made Jerusalem his capital and brought the ark. Solomon built the Temple.

test.q: How do Jewish and Christian traditions differ in reading the promise to David in 2 Samuel 7?
choices: Jewish tradition hopes for a future king from David's line; Christian tradition says Jesus is that king
Both say Solomon was that king and the promise ended
test.why: Both traditions read the same chapter as a promise about David's line, but they differ on who fulfills it.

test.q: Why did Nathan tell David a story about a lamb?
choices: To explain the rules for sacrifice
To lead David to judge his own wrong
test.why: 2 Samuel 12: David condemned the rich man, and Nathan said, You are the man.

test.q: What did Solomon ask for in his dream at Gibeon?
choices: An understanding heart to judge the people
test.why: 1 Kings 3 says Solomon asked for wisdom to judge. The text says riches and honor were added.

test.q: About when do many scholars place the split of the kingdom?
test.why: The split after Solomon's death is usually placed around 930 BCE. 722 and 586 BCE are the falls of Israel and Judah.

test.q: What was Deuteronomy 17's test for a king, which the books of Kings use for every ruler?
choices: Did he keep the covenant and the law?
test.why: Deuteronomy 17 says a king must read the law daily and keep it. Kings gives each ruler a short report on that.

write.prompt: What did these books say a good leader was? Choose two or three passages from the unit, such as Joshua 1:9, Judges 21:25, Ruth 1:16, 1 Samuel 16:7 or 1 Kings 3:9. Say what each passage says about a leader. Then explain how Jewish readers, Christian readers or scholars have read it. Use your own words.
tips: Name each passage by book, chapter and verse.
Say the story says or the text says. Do not tell the reader what to believe.
When you describe a belief, say whose it is: Jewish tradition, Christian tradition, many scholars.
Compare two readings instead of picking a winner.
Use the unit's words: judge, covenant, anoint, prophet, hesed.

title: The Land, the Judges and the Kings

chapters.title: Joshua, Judges and Ruth
chapters.bigQuestion: What do the stories of Joshua, Judges and Ruth show about what a people valued?

story.title: Where You Go, I Will Go
story.kicker: On a dusty road, a young widow makes a promise that changes a family's story.
paragraphs: The book of Ruth opens with a hard time. There is no food in the land of Judah. A family from Bethlehem moves to the country of Moab to find bread. The father dies there. The two sons marry women from Moab. Then, the story says, the two sons die too. Three widows are left: Naomi and her daughters-in-law, Orpah and Ruth.

Naomi hears that there is food again in Judah. She decides to walk home. On the road she stops. She tells the two young women to go back to their mothers. She has nothing to give them. She kisses them. All three of them cry. Orpah kisses Naomi goodbye and turns back toward Moab.

Ruth does not turn back. She holds on to Naomi. The story gives her a famous speech. Do not ask me to leave you, she says. Where you go, I will go. Where you sleep, I will sleep. Your people will be my people. Your God will be my God. Where you die, I will die.

Naomi sees that Ruth means it. She stops arguing. The two women walk on to Bethlehem together. Ruth is a foreigner there. She has no husband and no field. But she has made a promise, and she keeps it. The rest of the short book shows what that promise leads to.

The book of Ruth is only four chapters long. Jewish readers hear it read aloud every year at the spring festival of Shavuot. Christian Bibles place it right after the book of Judges. Both groups have loved it for the same reason. It is a story about loyalty and kindness between two people who had almost nothing.
story.think: Ruth chooses to stay with Naomi when she could have gone home. What do you think made her choose that?

lessons.title: A New Leader Named Joshua
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Joshua begins where Deuteronomy ends, with a new leader told to be strong and to keep the Torah.
reading: The book of Joshua is the sixth book of the Bible. It comes right after the five books of the *Torah*. Deuteronomy ends with the death of Moses. Joshua begins the very next moment. The people are camped by the Jordan River. The land of Canaan is on the other side. The story says God speaks to Joshua, the helper of Moses. Joshua is now the leader.

The first chapter gives Joshua a job and a rule. The job is to lead the people across the river. The rule is to keep the book of the law and think about it day and night. The text repeats one line three times. Be strong and of good courage. Do not be afraid. Readers have noticed that the new leader is told to be brave before anything else happens.

Jewish tradition places Joshua in a group of books called the Former Prophets. Christian Bibles call Joshua, Judges, Ruth and the books that follow the Historical Books. Both names tell us something. These books tell a story in order. Many scholars also think the books were written down long after the events they describe.

words.d: the first five books of the Bible; the word also means teaching
the Jewish name for Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings
the Christian name for Joshua through Esther, which tell a story in order

look.title: Be Strong and of Good Courage
look.text: Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.
look.prompt: This verse uses old words like thee and whithersoever. Say it again in your own words. Who is speaking, and to whom?

check.q: Which book comes right before Joshua in the Bible?
check.why: Deuteronomy is the last book of the Torah. It ends with the death of Moses, and Joshua begins right after.

check.q: What rule is Joshua given in chapter 1?
choices: Keep the book of the law and think about it day and night
Choose a king for the people
check.why: Joshua 1 tells Joshua to keep the law and think on it day and night. The temple and the king come much later.

check.q: What does Jewish tradition call the group of books that includes Joshua?
check.why: Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings are the Former Prophets in the Hebrew Bible. The Torah is the five books before them.

lessons.title: The Walls of Jericho
lessons.mainIdea: Joshua 6 tells how the people marched around Jericho for seven days, and readers of every kind have asked what the story means.
reading: Jericho was a walled city near the Jordan River. Joshua 2 says two spies went in first. A woman named Rahab hid them on her roof. She asked them to keep her family safe. They agreed. Then Joshua 6 tells the famous part. The people marched around the city once a day for six days. Priests carried the ark and blew trumpets made from rams' horns.

On the seventh day they marched around seven times. The priests blew the horns. Everyone shouted. The story says the wall fell down flat, and the people took the city. Rahab and her family were kept safe, just as the spies promised. The text says the city itself was destroyed.

This is a hard story, and readers have read it in many ways. Some Jewish and Christian readers take it as history. Many scholars think it was written long after, to teach a lesson about trust. Diggers at the site of Jericho disagree about what they found. They also disagree about when the walls fell. A public-school class can read the story as a story. It can notice what the story wants its readers to feel.

words.d: in Joshua, a gold-covered wooden chest the priests carried; the text says it held the tablets of the law
people sent secretly to look at a place before others go there

look.title: Seven Days Around a City
look.text: Picture the scene from Joshua 6. A walled city. Every morning, a long line of people walks all the way around it and says nothing. Priests blow rams' horns. Inside the walls, people watch from the top. On the seventh day the line goes around seven times, and then everyone shouts at once.
look.prompt: The story uses the number seven again and again. Where else in the Bible have you seen the number seven? Why might a storyteller repeat it?

check.q: How many times did the people march around Jericho on the seventh day?
check.why: Joshua 6 says the people marched once a day for six days and seven times on the seventh day.

check.q: Who hid the two spies in Jericho?
check.why: Joshua 2 says Rahab hid the spies on her roof. Deborah, Ruth and Naomi belong to other books.

check.q: How do many scholars read the Jericho story?
choices: As a poem that Moses sang
As a story written down long after the events, to teach a lesson
As a letter to a church
check.why: Many scholars think the story was written long after the time it describes. Some Jewish and Christian readers read it as history. Both readings exist.

lessons.title: Twelve Tribes, One Land
lessons.mainIdea: Joshua says the land was divided among twelve tribes, each named for a son or grandson of Jacob.
reading: Genesis says Jacob had twelve sons. Their families grew into twelve *tribes*. A tribe is a very large family group with its own name. The second half of the book of Joshua is mostly a map in words. It says which tribe got which part of the land. Many chapters are lists of towns and borders. They are not exciting to read. But they show how much the land mattered.

Two of the tribes are named for Joseph's sons, Ephraim and Manasseh. That keeps the number at twelve because one tribe, Levi, got no land of its own. The Levites served as priests and helpers at the place of worship. Joshua 21 says they lived in towns spread among the other tribes. Their job was their share.

The text also names cities of refuge. A person who killed someone by accident could run there and be safe until a fair trial. Jewish readers have studied these rules for many centuries. Christian readers have too. Both groups notice that the land is given with rules about being fair.

words.d: a very large family group with its own name; the Bible counts twelve tribes of Israel
the tribe of Levi, who served at the place of worship instead of holding land
a town where a person who caused a death by accident could stay safe until a trial

look.title: How Long Are These Books?
look.cite: Chapter counts in the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Ruth is the shortest book here. Why might a very short book still be one of the most read?

check.q: Which tribe got no land of its own in Joshua?
check.why: Joshua says the Levites served at the place of worship and lived in towns among the other tribes.

check.q: Ephraim and Manasseh were named for the two sons of which man?
check.why: Genesis names Ephraim and Manasseh as Joseph's sons. Counting them as tribes keeps the number at twelve.

check.q: What was a city of refuge for?
choices: A safe place for a person who caused a death by accident
A city where only kings lived
check.why: Joshua 20 describes cities of refuge as safe places until a fair trial could be held.

lessons.title: Choose This Day
lessons.mainIdea: Joshua 24 ends the book with the people gathered at Shechem, renewing their covenant.
reading: The book of Joshua ends with a big meeting. Joshua is old. He gathers all the tribes at a town called Shechem. He tells the whole story again from Abraham to that day. Then he gives the people a choice. Serve the God who brought you out of Egypt, or serve other gods. He says his own choice out loud. As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.

The people answer that they will serve too. Joshua warns them that it will be hard. They say it again. Then he makes a *covenant* with them. A covenant is a promise with rules on both sides. He writes it in the book of the law and sets up a large stone as a witness. Then the book says Joshua dies at the age of 110.

Readers have noticed that this scene echoes Mount Sinai. There the story says Moses gave the people the law. Here Joshua asks them to choose it again. Jewish and Christian readers both see a pattern. Each new generation has to say yes for itself. Many scholars think this scene was written to teach that lesson.

words.d: a binding promise with rules on both sides; in the Hebrew Bible, the bond between God and Israel
a town in the hills where Joshua gathered the tribes at the end of his life

look.title: A Stone as a Witness
look.text: In Joshua 24, the story says Joshua wrote the people's promise in the book of the law. Then he took a large stone and set it up under an oak tree near the place of worship. He told the people the stone had heard every word they said. It would be a witness against them if they broke their promise.
look.cite: Joshua 24:25–27, told in simple words from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Why set up a stone? What does a stone do that a spoken promise cannot?

check.q: Where did Joshua gather the tribes at the end of the book?
check.why: Joshua 24 says the meeting was at Shechem. Jerusalem becomes important later, under David.

check.q: What is a covenant?
choices: A promise with rules on both sides
check.why: A covenant is a binding agreement. In Joshua 24 the people promise to serve God and God's rules are set down.

check.q: Which earlier scene does Joshua 24 echo, according to many readers?
choices: The giving of the law at Mount Sinai
check.why: At Sinai the story says the people first accepted the law. At Shechem Joshua asks a new generation to choose it again.

lessons.title: What a Judge Was
lessons.mainIdea: In the book of Judges, a judge is not a person in a courtroom but a leader who rises up in a crisis.
reading: The book of Judges comes after Joshua. Its name can confuse readers. A *judge* in this book is not someone in a courtroom with a robe. A judge is a leader who steps up when the people are in trouble. The text says God raised up these leaders. Some led armies. Some settled arguments. The book names twelve of them.

Judges 2 explains the pattern of the whole book. The people forget the covenant. Enemies attack them. The people cry out for help. A judge rises up and saves them. Then there is peace for a while. Then the people forget again. Readers call this the *cycle* of Judges, because it goes around and around.

There was no king in this period. The last verse of the book says so. It adds that everyone did what was right in their own eyes. Some readers take that as a complaint. Others take it as a plain description. Many scholars think the writer wanted readers to see why a king came next, in the book of Samuel.

words.d: in the book of Judges, a leader who rises up to rescue the people in a time of trouble
a pattern that repeats; in Judges, forgetting, trouble, crying out, rescue, peace, and forgetting again

look.title: Around and Around
look.text: Draw a circle in your mind with five stops on it. Stop one: the people forget the covenant. Stop two: an enemy attacks. Stop three: the people cry out. Stop four: a judge rescues them. Stop five: peace for a time. Then the circle starts over. The book of Judges goes around that circle many times.
look.prompt: Why might a writer tell the same pattern over and over instead of once? What does the reader learn from the repeating?

check.q: In the book of Judges, what is a judge?
choices: A leader who rises up to rescue the people in a crisis
A person in a courtroom with a robe
A king who rules from a palace
A priest who serves at the ark
check.why: Judges are leaders raised up in trouble. Kings come later, in Samuel, and priests are a different role.

check.q: Which step comes right after the people cry out, in the cycle of Judges?
choices: A judge rises up and rescues them
check.why: Judges 2 sets the pattern: forgetting, attack, crying out, rescue, then peace.

check.q: What does the last verse of Judges say about a king?
choices: There was no king in Israel
check.why: Judges 21:25 says there was no king in those days. Saul and David come in the book of Samuel.

lessons.title: Deborah Under the Palm Tree
lessons.mainIdea: Deborah is a judge and a prophet who sits under a palm tree, settles disputes and sends a general to war.
reading: Judges 4 introduces Deborah. The text calls her a *prophet*, a person who speaks a message from God. It also says she judged Israel. People came to her to settle their arguments. She sat under a palm tree in the hill country between two towns. She is the only judge in the book who is described this way, doing the work of a judge in the everyday sense.

A king named Jabin had nine hundred iron chariots. His general was Sisera. The story says Deborah sent for a man named Barak. She told him to take ten thousand men to Mount Tabor. Barak said he would go only if she went too. She agreed, but told him the honor would go to a woman. The chariots got stuck, and Sisera ran away on foot.

Sisera hid in the tent of a woman named Jael. She killed him while he slept. Judges 5 then tells the whole story again as a song. Many scholars think this song is one of the oldest pieces of writing in the Bible. Jewish and Christian readers alike have pointed to Deborah as a leader of unusual strength.

words.d: a person who speaks a message from God; Deborah is called a prophet in Judges 4
a two-wheeled cart pulled by horses and used in battle

look.title: Two Tellings of One Battle
look.text: Judges 4 tells the story of Deborah and Barak in plain prose, like a report. Judges 5 tells it again as a song, with Deborah and Barak singing. The song names the tribes who came to fight and the tribes who stayed home. It even imagines Sisera's mother at a window, waiting for him.
look.prompt: Why might the Bible keep both a prose version and a song version of the same event? What can a song do that a report cannot?

check.q: Where did Deborah sit to settle disputes?
choices: Under a palm tree in the hill country
check.why: Judges 4:5 says Deborah sat under a palm tree and the people came to her for judgment.

check.q: Which word does Judges 4 use for Deborah besides judge?
check.why: Judges 4:4 calls Deborah a prophet. Queens and priests are other roles, and spies belong to the Jericho story.

check.q: What is Judges 5?
choices: The story of the battle told again as a song
check.why: Judges 5 is the Song of Deborah. Many scholars think it is one of the oldest passages in the Bible.

lessons.title: Gideon's Small Army
lessons.mainIdea: The story of Gideon shrinks an army from thousands to three hundred to make a point about who wins the battle.
reading: Judges 6 finds Gideon hiding wheat from raiders called the Midianites. The story says a messenger from God calls him a mighty man of valor. Gideon does not feel mighty. He asks for signs. He puts out a sheep's fleece and asks for dew on it but not the ground. Then he asks for the opposite. The text says both happen. Gideon is a leader who needs to be sure.

Judges 7 is the famous part. Gideon gathers a big army. The story says God tells him it is too big. If they win, they will say they did it themselves. Everyone who is afraid may go home. Most leave. Then the men drink at a stream. Only those who lap water with their hands are kept. Three hundred remain.

That night the three hundred surround the enemy camp with trumpets, jars and torches. They break the jars, wave the torches and shout. The camp panics. Readers have drawn different lessons. Some see a story about trust. Some see a story about a small group beating a large one. Many scholars think the shrinking numbers are the storyteller's main point.

words.d: raiders from the east who, Judges says, took the crops of Israel in Gideon's time
the wool of a sheep; Gideon used one to ask for a sign

look.title: Gideon's Shrinking Army
rows: Men who stayed after the afraid went home
Men kept after the test at the stream
look.prompt: The numbers go down each time. What does the text say is the reason for sending men home? What is the storyteller trying to show?

check.q: How many men did Gideon keep after the test at the stream?
check.why: Judges 7:7 says three hundred men were kept. Nine hundred is the number of Jabin's chariots in the Deborah story.

check.q: Why does the story say the army had to be made smaller?
choices: The enemy asked for a fair fight
So the people would not say they won by their own strength
check.why: Judges 7:2 gives the reason: a big army would take the credit for itself.

check.q: What did Gideon use to ask for a sign?
check.why: Judges 6 tells of the fleece and the dew. The ram's horn belongs to Jericho and the stone to Joshua 24.

lessons.title: Samson's Strength
lessons.mainIdea: Samson is the strongest judge and one of the weakest at keeping promises, and his story ends the book's list of leaders.
reading: Judges 13 to 16 tell about Samson. Before he is born, a messenger tells his mother he will be a *Nazirite*. That is a person set apart by a vow. A Nazirite does not drink wine, touch a dead body or cut his hair. The story says Samson's strength is tied to that vow. He fights the Philistines, a people who lived along the coast.

Samson does amazing things in the story. He tears a lion apart. He carries off a city gate. He breaks every rope that ties him. But he also breaks his own rules again and again. He tells his secret to a woman named Delilah. She has his hair cut while he sleeps. The Philistines capture him and blind him.

At the end, his hair grows back. In a great hall, he pushes the pillars apart and the roof falls on everyone, himself too. Readers have never agreed about Samson. Some see a hero. Some see a warning. Jewish tradition and Christian tradition both list him among the judges. Many scholars think his story shows the cycle of Judges winding down toward a need for something new.

words.d: a person set apart by a vow who does not drink wine, touch a dead body or cut his hair
a people who lived along the coast and often fought Israel in Judges and Samuel

look.title: No King in Israel
look.text: In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.
look.prompt: This is the last line of the book. Is it a complaint, a description or a hint about what comes next? Say which you think and why.

check.q: What is a Nazirite?
choices: A person set apart by a vow, who does not cut his hair
A judge who sits under a tree
A spy sent into a city
check.why: Judges 13 explains the Nazirite vow. Samson's story says his strength is tied to it.

check.q: Who were the Philistines?
choices: Raiders from the east in Gideon's time
Priests from the tribe of Levi
A people who lived along the coast
check.why: The Philistines lived on the coast and fought Israel in Judges and Samuel. The Midianites were the eastern raiders.

check.q: How does the book of Judges end?
choices: With the building of the Temple
With the line that there was no king and everyone did what was right in their own eyes
check.why: Judges 21:25 is the last verse. Joshua's death ends the book of Joshua, and David comes in Samuel.

lessons.title: Ruth and Naomi
lessons.mainIdea: Ruth is a foreigner from Moab who chooses to stay with Naomi, and her words became one of the Bible's best-loved promises.
reading: The book of Ruth says it takes place in the days when the judges ruled. Naomi is from Bethlehem. She loses her husband and both sons in *Moab*, a country east of the Dead Sea. Her daughter-in-law Ruth is a Moabite. In other parts of the Bible, Moab is an enemy. That makes Ruth's story surprising from the first page.

Naomi tells Ruth to go home. Ruth refuses. Her speech in Ruth 1:16 has been read at weddings and funerals for centuries. She promises to go where Naomi goes and to make Naomi's people and God her own. The two women arrive in Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest. Naomi says she left full and came back empty.

The book is short and quiet. Nobody fights a battle. God does not speak out loud. Instead, people are kind to each other. The Hebrew word for this kindness is *hesed*. Jewish readers often say the whole book is about hesed. Christian readers have said the same thing in their own words.

words.d: a country east of the Dead Sea; Ruth came from there
a Hebrew word for loyal kindness that goes beyond what is required
the wife of a person's son

look.title: Where You Go, I Will Go
look.text: Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.
look.prompt: Count the promises Ruth makes in this one sentence. Which one do you think was hardest to keep?

check.q: Where was Ruth from?
check.why: Ruth was a Moabite. Naomi was from Bethlehem, and the two women traveled there together.

check.q: What does the Hebrew word hesed mean?
choices: Loyal kindness beyond what is required
check.why: Hesed is loyal kindness. Many readers say it is the main idea of the book of Ruth.

check.q: When does the book of Ruth say its story takes place?
choices: In the time of King David
In the days when the judges ruled
check.why: Ruth 1:1 sets the story in the days of the judges, which is why the book sits after Judges in Christian Bibles.

lessons.title: A Field, a Wedding and a King
lessons.mainIdea: Ruth gathers grain in the field of Boaz, marries him, and the book ends by naming her as the great-grandmother of David.
reading: Ruth goes out to find food. She gathers leftover grain behind the harvest workers. This is called *gleaning*. The Torah, in Leviticus 19, says farmers must leave the edges of the field and the dropped grain for the poor and the stranger. Ruth is both. The field belongs to a kind man named Boaz. He tells his workers to leave extra for her.

Boaz is a relative of Naomi's husband. Naomi sees a chance. In the book's rules, a close relative can marry a widow and keep the family's land in the family. Boaz agrees, in front of the town leaders at the gate. He and Ruth marry. They have a son named Obed. The women of the town say a son has been born to Naomi.

The last lines of the book are a family list. Obed was the father of Jesse. Jesse was the father of David. So the foreigner from Moab is the great-grandmother of Israel's most famous king. Jewish readers read the book each year at Shavuot, the harvest festival. The Gospel of Matthew, in the New Testament, also names Ruth in the family line of Jesus.

words.d: gathering leftover grain after the harvest, which the Torah says must be left for the poor and the stranger
a Jewish spring harvest festival when the book of Ruth is read aloud

look.title: Why This Story?
look.text: The book of Ruth is a story about two poor widows, a field and a wedding. There is no battle and no miracle. Yet it was kept, copied and read for thousands of years. One clue is the ending, which connects Ruth to King David. Another clue is the kindness that every character shows.
look.prompt: Think about what a people chooses to keep and retell. What does keeping the book of Ruth tell you about what its readers valued?

check.q: What is gleaning?
choices: Setting up a stone as a witness
Sitting under a palm tree to judge
Gathering leftover grain after the harvest
check.why: Ruth 2 shows Ruth gleaning. Leviticus 19 says the leftovers must be left for the poor and the stranger.

check.q: Who was Ruth's great-grandson, according to the end of the book?
check.why: Ruth 4 ends with the line Obed, Jesse, David. Samson, Joshua and Gideon are leaders from earlier books.

check.q: At which festival do Jewish communities read the book of Ruth?
check.why: Ruth is read at Shavuot, the harvest festival. Esther is the book read at Purim.

review.q: Which book tells about Deborah, Gideon and Samson?
review.why: Deborah, Gideon and Samson are judges in the book of Judges.

review.q: What did Joshua set up at Shechem as a witness to the people's promise?
review.why: Joshua 24:26 says he set up a large stone under an oak as a witness.

review.q: Which of these is the shortest book in this chapter?
review.why: Ruth has four chapters. Joshua has 24, Judges 21 and 1 Samuel 31.

review.q: What is the cycle of Judges?
choices: Forgetting, trouble, crying out, rescue and peace, repeated
The family line from Ruth to David
review.why: Judges 2 lays out the repeating pattern that the rest of the book follows.

review.q: How do Jewish readers and Christian readers differ in where they place the book of Ruth?
choices: Jewish Bibles put it in the Writings; Christian Bibles put it after Judges
review.why: In the Hebrew Bible Ruth is among the Writings and read at Shavuot. Christian Bibles place it after Judges.

review.q: Which leader asked for a sign with a sheep's fleece?
review.why: Judges 6 tells how Gideon put out a fleece and asked for dew on it.

review.q: Which tribe served at the place of worship instead of holding land?
review.why: Joshua 21 says the Levites lived in towns spread among the other tribes.

review.q: How does the book of Ruth end?
choices: With a family list that leads to David
With Samson in the great hall
review.why: Ruth 4 ends with the names Obed, Jesse and David.

chapters.title: Samuel, Saul, David and Solomon
chapters.bigQuestion: What did the books of Samuel and Kings say a king was supposed to be, and how did the first kings measure up?

story.title: One Baby, Two Mothers and a Sword
story.kicker: A new king faces a case with no witnesses, and the whole country waits to see what he will do.
paragraphs: The first book of Kings tells about a young king named Solomon. He has just become king after his father, David. Early in his reign, the story says, two women come to him with a problem. They live in the same house. Each had a baby a few days apart. There was no one else in the house. Now one baby is dead, and both women say the living baby is theirs.

The first woman speaks. She says the other woman rolled over on her own baby in the night. Then, while it was still dark, the other woman switched the babies. The first woman woke up to feed her son and found a dead child in her arms. In the morning light, she looked closely. It was not her son.

The second woman says no. The living child is hers. The dead child belongs to the first woman. They argue in front of the king. There are no witnesses. There is no proof. The whole court watches to see what the new king will do.

Solomon asks for a sword. He says he will cut the living baby in two and give half to each woman. The first woman cries out at once. Give her the baby, she says. Do not hurt him. The second woman says, let it be neither mine nor yours. Cut him.

Solomon gives the baby to the first woman. She is the mother, he says. She would rather lose him than see him hurt. The story says all Israel heard about the case. They saw that the king had wisdom to judge. Jewish and Christian readers have retold this story for nearly three thousand years. It is their picture of a wise ruler. In this chapter you will meet the kings who came before Solomon. You will also see what happened after him.
story.think: Solomon never meant to use the sword. What did he really want to find out, and why did his plan work?

lessons.title: Hannah's Prayer and Samuel
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Samuel begins with a mother's prayer, and her son Samuel becomes the last of the judges and the maker of kings.
reading: The books of Samuel are named for a man, but they begin with his mother. Hannah has no children. She goes to the place of worship at Shiloh and prays so hard that the priest, Eli, thinks she is drunk. She promises that if she has a son, she will give him back to serve God. The story says her prayer is answered. She names the boy *Samuel*.

When Samuel is still small, Hannah brings him to Shiloh to live with Eli. One night, the text says, a voice calls his name. Three times Samuel runs to Eli. Three times Eli says he did not call. Then Eli understands. He tells the boy to answer, Speak, for your servant is listening. Samuel grows up to be a *prophet*, a judge and the leader of the people.

In the Hebrew Bible, Samuel is one book. Christian Bibles split it into 1 Samuel and 2 Samuel because of its length. The same is true of Kings. Hannah's song of thanks in 1 Samuel 2 is about God lifting up the poor and bringing down the proud. Jewish readers read it in the synagogue on the New Year. Christian readers have noticed how much Mary's song in Luke sounds like it.

words.d: the prophet and judge who anointed the first two kings of Israel; two books of the Bible carry his name
a person who speaks a message from God
the town where the place of worship stood before the Temple was built

look.title: One Book or Two?
look.text: In the Hebrew Bible, Samuel is one book and Kings is one book. In Christian Bibles they are 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings and 2 Kings. The words are the same. Only the dividing is different. Many scholars think the split happened when the books were translated into Greek, because Greek takes up more space on a scroll.
look.prompt: If you cut one long book into two, where would you cut it? Look at how 1 Samuel ends and 2 Samuel begins, and say whether that was a good place.

check.q: Who was Samuel's mother?
check.why: 1 Samuel 1 tells of Hannah's prayer at Shiloh. Ruth, Deborah and Naomi belong to earlier books.

check.q: Why do Christian Bibles have a 1 Samuel and a 2 Samuel?
choices: Two different men named Samuel wrote them
One is in Hebrew and one in Greek
The second one was found later
One long book was split in two because of its length
check.why: Samuel is one book in the Hebrew Bible. It was divided in two when it was copied into Greek, most scholars think.

check.q: What did Eli tell Samuel to say when the voice called?
choices: Speak, for your servant is listening
Be strong and of good courage
Where you go, I will go
check.why: 1 Samuel 3 gives Samuel this answer. The other lines belong to Joshua, Ruth and the elders of Israel.

lessons.title: Give Us a King
lessons.mainIdea: In 1 Samuel 8, the people ask for a king like other nations, and Samuel warns them what a king will cost.
reading: Samuel grows old. His sons are judges, but they take bribes. The leaders of the people come to Samuel with a request. Give us a king to rule us, like all the other nations. The text says Samuel is unhappy. He prays. The story says God tells him the people are not rejecting Samuel but rejecting God as their king. Still, Samuel is told to give them what they ask.

First he warns them. A king will take your sons for his army and his chariots. He will take your daughters to cook and bake. He will take the best of your fields and a tenth of your grain. You will cry out, and it will be too late. The people listen and say it anyway. We want a king. Samuel sends them home.

The Torah had already given rules for a king in Deuteronomy 17. A king must not gather many horses or many wives. He must not pile up silver and gold. He must write his own copy of the law and read it every day. Jewish and Christian readers both use these rules to measure the kings who follow. Many scholars think the books of Samuel and Kings were written to do exactly that.

words.d: to pour oil on a person's head as a sign that they are chosen for a job, such as king or priest
money or a gift given to make a judge decide unfairly

look.title: Like All the Nations
look.text: In 1 Samuel 8, the elders tell Samuel that he is old and his sons do not follow his ways. They ask him to give them a king to judge them, the way all the other nations have. Samuel does not like the request. He prays, and the story says he is told to listen to the people but to warn them first.
look.cite: 1 Samuel 8:4–9, told in simple words from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: The elders give two reasons for wanting a king. What are they? Which reason do you think mattered more to them?

check.q: What did the elders ask Samuel for in 1 Samuel 8?
choices: A king, like the other nations
check.why: The elders asked for a king to rule them like all the nations. The temple comes later, under Solomon.

check.q: Which was one of Samuel's warnings about a king?
choices: He will make everyone a priest
He will give the land back to Egypt
He will take your sons, your fields and a tenth of your grain
check.why: 1 Samuel 8 lists what a king will take: sons, daughters, fields and a tenth of the crops.

check.q: What does Deuteronomy 17 say a king must do?
choices: Write his own copy of the law and read it
check.why: Deuteronomy 17 says a king must write out the law and read it daily, and must not gather horses, wives or gold.

lessons.title: Saul, the First King
lessons.mainIdea: Saul is tall, brave and chosen, but the story says he loses his place as king by not following instructions.
reading: The first king is a young man named Saul from the tribe of Benjamin. 1 Samuel 9 says he was taller than anyone else in the land. He was out looking for his father's lost donkeys when he met Samuel. Samuel poured oil on his head. This is called *anointing*, and it marked him as the chosen one. Later Samuel showed him to all the people, and they shouted, Long live the king.

Saul wins battles against the Ammonites and the Philistines. His son Jonathan is a brave fighter too. But the story tells of two times when Saul does not do what Samuel tells him. Once he offers a sacrifice himself instead of waiting for Samuel. Once he does not carry out an order fully after a battle. Samuel tells him that God has rejected him as king.

After this, the text says, Saul's mood grows dark. He becomes jealous and afraid. Readers have felt sorry for Saul for a long time. He did not ask to be king. Some Jewish and Christian readers see a tragic figure. Others see a warning about obeying. The text lets readers hold both.

words.d: the smallest tribe of Israel; Saul came from it
an animal or gift offered to God at an altar, according to the rules of the Torah

look.title: A King Who Did Not Ask
look.text: Saul was looking for lost donkeys when Samuel found him. When it was time to show him to the people, the story says Saul was hiding among the baggage. He had to be pulled out. Later, the same Saul leads armies and wins. Later still, he loses his place as king and grows jealous of a shepherd boy.
look.prompt: Is Saul's story a sad story or a warning story? Point to one thing in the text that supports your answer.

check.q: From which tribe did Saul come?
check.why: 1 Samuel 9 says Saul was a Benjaminite. David came from Judah.

check.q: What does it mean to anoint someone?
choices: To pour oil on their head as a sign they are chosen
To write their name in the law
check.why: Samuel poured oil on Saul's head. Anointing marked a person as chosen for a role.

check.q: What was Saul doing when he first met Samuel?
choices: Looking for his father's lost donkeys
check.why: 1 Samuel 9 tells how Saul went out looking for donkeys and met the prophet instead.

lessons.title: A Shepherd Is Chosen
lessons.mainIdea: Samuel goes to Bethlehem and anoints the youngest son of Jesse, a shepherd boy named David.
reading: 1 Samuel 16 sends Samuel to Bethlehem, the town of Ruth and Boaz. He is to find a new king among the sons of a man named *Jesse*. Jesse brings out his oldest son. He is tall and handsome. Samuel thinks this must be the one. The story says God tells him no. People look at the outside. God looks at the heart.

Seven sons pass by. None is chosen. Samuel asks if there are any more. Jesse says the youngest is out with the sheep. They send for him. He is a boy named *David*. The text says he had a healthy glow and beautiful eyes. Samuel anoints him in front of his brothers. Then David goes back to the sheep.

Later in the same chapter, King Saul is troubled and cannot rest. His servants suggest music. Someone knows a shepherd from Bethlehem who plays the harp well. David comes to the palace and plays for the king. Saul feels better. Jewish tradition connects David with the book of Psalms, and 73 psalms carry his name in their titles. Christian readers sing those psalms too.

words.d: a man of Bethlehem, the grandson of Ruth and the father of David
the shepherd from Bethlehem who became the second king of Israel
a song or poem of prayer; the book of Psalms has 150 of them

look.title: The Outside and the Heart
look.text: But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
look.prompt: Countenance means face. Stature means height. Put this verse in your own words. Why does the story include it before David appears?

check.q: In which town did Samuel find David?
check.why: 1 Samuel 16 sends Samuel to Bethlehem, the same town as Ruth and Boaz.

check.q: What was David doing when his brothers were shown to Samuel?
check.why: Jesse said the youngest was out with the sheep. Hiding among the baggage was Saul.

check.q: Why was David first brought to Saul's palace?
choices: To play music that calmed the king
check.why: 1 Samuel 16 says Saul's servants sent for a harp player, and David's music helped the king rest.

lessons.title: David and Goliath
lessons.mainIdea: The story of David and Goliath is about a small, unarmed boy who trusts, facing a giant who mocks.
reading: 1 Samuel 17 is one of the best-known stories in the Bible. The Philistine army camps on one hill. Saul's army camps on another. In the valley between them, a huge soldier named *Goliath* from the city of Gath steps out every day. He wears bronze armor and carries a heavy spear. He shouts for one man to come and fight him. For forty days no one does.

David's father sends him to bring food to his brothers. David hears the shout and asks why no one answers. His oldest brother is angry. Saul says David is only a boy. David answers that he has fought a lion and a bear to protect his sheep. Saul lets him go. David tries on Saul's armor and takes it off. He picks five smooth stones from the stream and walks out with his *sling*.

Goliath laughs at him. David says he comes in the name of God, not with a sword. He whirls the sling. The stone strikes Goliath's forehead, and he falls. The Philistines run. Readers of every kind have used this story as a picture of the small against the large. Jewish readers, Christian readers and many with no religion all say a David and Goliath contest.

words.d: the giant Philistine soldier from Gath whom David faced in the valley of Elah
a strap used to whirl and throw a stone hard and fast; shepherds used it to guard sheep

look.title: How Tall Was Goliath?
look.text: The Hebrew text used by the King James Version says Goliath was six cubits and a span tall. A cubit is about 18 inches, so that is over nine feet. But some very old copies, including a Dead Sea Scroll and the ancient Greek translation, say four cubits and a span, about six and a half feet. Scholars still discuss which number is older.
look.prompt: Why might a copyist make a giant taller over time, or shorter? Does the size change what the story means?

check.q: Which city was Goliath from?
check.why: 1 Samuel 17:4 says Goliath was from Gath, a Philistine city.

check.q: What did David say he had done that showed he could fight?
choices: Fought a lion and a bear to protect his sheep
check.why: David told Saul about the lion and the bear. He had not yet fought in any battle.

check.q: Why do some old copies of the story give a different height for Goliath?
choices: Ancient copies of the text do not all agree, and scholars discuss which is older
The King James Version made up the number
Goliath grew during the forty days
The Greek translation left him out
check.why: The Hebrew text and some older witnesses give different numbers. That is a normal question for scholars who compare manuscripts.

lessons.title: David and Jonathan
lessons.mainIdea: Jonathan, the king's son, becomes David's closest friend and protects him from his own father's jealousy.
reading: After Goliath, David becomes a hero. Women sing that Saul has killed thousands and David tens of thousands. Saul hears the song and grows jealous. The story says he throws a spear at David twice while David plays the harp. But Saul's own son *Jonathan* loves David like himself. The text says the two make a *covenant* of friendship. Jonathan gives David his robe, his sword and his bow.

1 Samuel 20 tells how Jonathan finds out that his father means to kill David. The two friends meet in a field. Jonathan shoots arrows as a secret signal. Then they weep together. Jonathan sends David away to save his life. David spends years hiding in caves and the wilderness. Twice he could have killed Saul and did not.

Saul and Jonathan both die in a battle against the Philistines on Mount Gilboa. 2 Samuel 1 gives David's song of grief for them. He says Jonathan's love was wonderful to him. Jewish and Christian readers have called this one of the closest friendships in the Bible. Many scholars add one more point. The covenant between them explains why David later cares for Jonathan's son.

words.d: Saul's son and David's closest friend, who died beside his father at Mount Gilboa
a binding promise with rules on both sides; David and Jonathan made one as friends

look.title: A Chance in a Cave
look.text: 1 Samuel 24 says Saul went into a cave alone. David and his men were hiding in the back of the same cave. David's men whispered that this was his chance. David crept up and quietly cut off a corner of Saul's robe. Then he felt bad even about that. When Saul left, David called after him and held up the piece of cloth to show what he could have done.
look.prompt: David could have ended his years of hiding in one moment. What does the story want readers to see about him by showing what he did not do?

check.q: Who was Jonathan?
choices: Saul's son and David's closest friend
check.why: Jonathan was Saul's son. He protected David from his father's jealousy.

check.q: What secret signal did Jonathan use in the field?
check.why: 1 Samuel 20 describes Jonathan shooting arrows as a signal. The piece of robe belongs to the cave story.

check.q: What did David do when he found Saul alone in a cave?
choices: He ran away without being seen
He cut off a corner of Saul's robe and let him go
check.why: 1 Samuel 24 says David cut the robe and spared Saul, then showed him the cloth.

lessons.title: King in Jerusalem
lessons.mainIdea: David becomes king of all Israel, makes Jerusalem his capital and brings the ark there, and the text says his family line will last.
reading: After Saul's death, 2 Samuel says David is made king at Hebron by his own tribe, Judah. Seven years later the other tribes ask him to rule them too. The text says he reigned forty years in all. David needed a capital that belonged to no tribe. He captured a hill city called *Jerusalem* from the Jebusites. Many scholars date this to about 1000 BCE.

David brings the *ark* to Jerusalem with music and dancing. 2 Samuel 6 says he danced so hard that his wife Michal was embarrassed for him. He wants to build a house for the ark. The prophet Nathan brings him a message in 2 Samuel 7. David will not build the house. Instead, the text says, God will build David a house, meaning a family line that lasts.

Jewish tradition reads this promise as the start of a hope. One day a king from David's line will come. Christian tradition reads the Gospels as saying that Jesus, born in Bethlehem, is that king. Both readings begin from the same chapter. A public-school class can hold both side by side. Each one grows out of the text.

words.d: the hill city David captured and made his capital, about 1000 BCE
the gold-covered chest carried by the priests; David brought it to Jerusalem
the town in Judah where David first became king

look.title: How Long Did They Reign?
look.unit: years, as the text counts them
look.cite: 2 Samuel 5:4–5 and 1 Kings 11:42, King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Both David and Solomon are given forty years. Forty is also the number of days of rain in Noah's story and years in the wilderness. What might the number mean in the Bible?

check.q: Where did David first become king?
check.why: 2 Samuel 2 says David was made king of Judah at Hebron. He moved to Jerusalem after the tribes joined him.

check.q: What did Nathan tell David in 2 Samuel 7?
choices: David would not build the house, but his family line would last
David would be replaced by Saul
check.why: 2 Samuel 7 says Solomon, not David, will build the house, and promises David a lasting line.

check.q: How do Jewish and Christian readers differ about the promise to David?
choices: Jewish readers say there was no promise
Christian readers do not read 2 Samuel
Jewish tradition hopes for a future king from David's line; Christian tradition says Jesus is that king
Both say Solomon was the last king
check.why: Both traditions read 2 Samuel 7 as a promise about David's line. They differ on who fulfills it.

lessons.title: Nathan's Story of the Lamb
lessons.mainIdea: The text does not hide David's worst deed, and a prophet's short story makes the king judge himself.
reading: 2 Samuel 11 tells a story the Bible could have left out. David sees a woman named Bathsheba bathing on a roof. He sends for her, though she is married to a soldier named Uriah. When she becomes pregnant, David tries to cover it up. Then he sends Uriah to the front of a battle, where he is killed. David marries Bathsheba. The text ends the chapter by saying that what David had done displeased God.

The prophet *Nathan* comes to the king. He tells a story. A rich man had many sheep. A poor man had one little lamb that he loved like a daughter. A traveler came to the rich man. The rich man would not use his own sheep. He took the poor man's lamb and cooked it. David is furious. That man deserves to die, he says.

Nathan answers with four words. You are the man. David sees it. He does not argue. He says, I have sinned. Jewish tradition connects Psalm 51, a prayer for a clean heart, to this moment. Christian readers do the same. Many scholars say this story shows what a *parable* can do. It lets a listener judge before he knows he is judging himself.

words.d: the prophet who told David the story of the lamb and gave him the promise about his family line
a short story that teaches by making the listener see something in a new way
the wife of Uriah, whom David took; later the mother of Solomon

look.title: Four Words
look.text: And Nathan said to David, Thou art the man.
look.prompt: Nathan waits until David has judged the rich man before he says this. Why did he not just tell David what he had done wrong?

check.q: In Nathan's story, what did the rich man take?
choices: The poor man's one little lamb
check.why: 2 Samuel 12 tells of the rich man who took the poor man's only lamb to feed a guest.

check.q: What is a parable?
choices: A short story that teaches by letting the listener see something new
check.why: Nathan's story is a parable. Jesus in the Gospels also teaches with parables.

check.q: How did David answer when Nathan said, You are the man?
choices: He said the story was not true
check.why: 2 Samuel 12:13 says David admitted his wrong at once. The text does not have him argue.

lessons.title: The Wise King
lessons.mainIdea: Solomon asks for wisdom instead of riches, and the story of the two mothers shows what that wisdom looked like.
reading: David grows old, and his son Solomon becomes king. 1 Kings 3 says Solomon goes to a high place called Gibeon to worship. That night he has a dream. The story says God asks him what he wants. Solomon does not ask for a long life or riches or the death of his enemies. He asks for an understanding heart to judge the people and to know good from bad.

The text says the answer pleases God. Solomon gets *wisdom*, and riches and honor besides. The very next story is the case of the two mothers and one baby. Solomon calls for a sword, and the real mother gives up her claim to save the child. The book says all Israel heard about it and saw that the king could judge.

1 Kings 4 says Solomon spoke three thousand *proverbs* and more than a thousand songs. A proverb is a short wise saying. Jewish tradition connects him with the book of Proverbs, and its first verse carries his name. Christian readers do too. Many scholars think the book grew over centuries, gathering sayings from many hands, and was placed under the name of the wise king.

words.d: good judgment; knowing what is right and what will happen if you do a thing
a short wise saying; the book of Proverbs is a collection of them
the high place where 1 Kings says Solomon had his dream

look.title: What Solomon Asked For
look.text: In 1 Kings 3, the story says God appears to Solomon in a dream at Gibeon and tells him to ask for whatever he wants. Solomon says he is only a young man who does not know how to go out or come in. He asks for an understanding heart so he can judge the people and tell good from bad. The text says God is pleased that he did not ask for long life, riches or victory over enemies.
look.cite: 1 Kings 3:5–13, told in simple words from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Solomon could have asked for anything. What does his choice tell you about what the book thinks a king is for?

check.q: What did Solomon ask for in his dream at Gibeon?
choices: An understanding heart to judge the people
check.why: 1 Kings 3 says Solomon asked for wisdom to judge. The text says he was given riches and honor besides.

check.q: How did Solomon find the real mother in the story of the two women?
choices: He looked at the baby's face
He offered to cut the baby in two, and the real mother gave up her claim
check.why: 1 Kings 3:16–28 tells the story. The real mother would rather lose the child than see him hurt.

check.q: Which book of the Bible does Jewish tradition connect with Solomon?
check.why: Proverbs 1:1 carries Solomon's name. Many scholars think the book gathered sayings over a long time.

lessons.title: The Temple in Jerusalem
lessons.mainIdea: Solomon builds the first Temple in Jerusalem, a stone and cedar house for the ark that took seven years to complete.
reading: David had wanted to build a house for the ark. The text says his son did it. 1 Kings 6 describes the *Temple* in detail. It was built of cut stone and lined with *cedar* wood from Lebanon, sent by King Hiram of Tyre. The inside was covered with gold. The innermost room held the ark. The book says the building took seven years.

The Temple was not a place where people sat in rows. Priests offered sacrifices in the courtyard outside. The people gathered there for festivals. 1 Kings 8 gives Solomon's long prayer on the day the Temple opened. He says that even the heavens cannot hold God, so how could this house. He asks that prayers said toward this place be heard, even from far away.

This building is called the First Temple. The Babylonians destroyed it in 586 BCE, a story told later in this course. A Second Temple was built after the exile and stood until the Romans destroyed it in 70 CE. Jewish tradition still turns toward Jerusalem in prayer. Christian and Muslim traditions also hold the city sacred. Nothing of Solomon's building can be seen today, and scholars debate its exact size and date.

words.d: the house of worship Solomon built in Jerusalem, where the priests served and the ark was kept
a tall evergreen tree from Lebanon; its wood lined Solomon's Temple
the king of Tyre who sent cedar and workers to help build the Temple

look.title: The Temple by the Numbers
rows: Length of the main building, in cubits
look.prompt: A cubit is about 18 inches. Work out the length of the Temple in feet. Is it bigger or smaller than your school gym?

check.q: Where did the cedar wood for the Temple come from?
check.why: 1 Kings 5 says King Hiram of Tyre sent cedar from Lebanon.

check.q: How many years did 1 Kings say the Temple took to build?
check.why: 1 Kings 6:38 says seven years. Forty is the length of David's and Solomon's reigns.

check.q: What happened to Solomon's Temple?
choices: The Romans destroyed it in 70 CE
The Babylonians destroyed it in 586 BCE
check.why: The First Temple fell to Babylon in 586 BCE. The Second Temple, built later, is the one the Romans destroyed in 70 CE.

lessons.title: One Kingdom Becomes Two
lessons.mainIdea: After Solomon dies, ten tribes break away, and the books of Kings measure every ruler by the rules for a king.
reading: 1 Kings 11 says Solomon's later years were troubled. He married many foreign wives, built places for their gods and taxed the people hard. Readers who remember Deuteronomy 17 notice that he broke its rules for a king. When he dies, his son *Rehoboam* goes to Shechem to be made king. The people ask him to make their load lighter.

Rehoboam asks the old advisors. They say, serve the people today and they will serve you forever. He asks his young friends instead. They tell him to say, my father made your load heavy and I will make it heavier. He says it. Ten tribes walk away and make a man named *Jeroboam* their king. Only Judah and Benjamin stay with Rehoboam. Many scholars date this split to about 930 BCE.

From now on there are two kingdoms. *Israel* in the north has its capital at Samaria in time. *Judah* in the south keeps Jerusalem and the Temple. The books of Kings follow both, ruler by ruler. Each king gets a short report card. Did he keep the covenant or not? Jewish and Christian readers both take this as the books' way of saying what a king was for.

words.d: Solomon's son, whose harsh answer at Shechem led ten tribes to break away
the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel after the split
after the split, the northern kingdom of ten tribes
after the split, the southern kingdom with Jerusalem and the Temple

look.title: Two Kinds of Advice
look.text: The old advisors tell Rehoboam to be a servant to the people for one day, and they will serve him for all their days. The young men tell him to say that his little finger is thicker than his father's waist. Rehoboam picks the second answer. 1 Kings 12 says the people reply, What share do we have in David? To your tents, Israel!
look.prompt: Put each piece of advice in your own words. What does the writer want readers to think about a king who takes the second kind?

check.q: What did the people ask Rehoboam at Shechem?
choices: To move the capital to Samaria
To go to war with Egypt
check.why: 1 Kings 12 says the people asked for lighter work and taxes. Rehoboam refused.

check.q: Who became king of the ten northern tribes?
check.why: Jeroboam led the northern kingdom of Israel. Nathan was a prophet, Hiram a king of Tyre, and Jonathan Saul's son.

check.q: After the split, which kingdom kept Jerusalem and the Temple?
check.why: Judah, with Benjamin, kept Jerusalem. Israel in the north came to have its capital at Samaria.

review.q: Who anointed both Saul and David as king?
review.why: Samuel anointed Saul in 1 Samuel 10 and David in 1 Samuel 16.

review.q: Which two books are one book each in the Hebrew Bible but two in Christian Bibles?
review.why: Samuel and Kings were each split in two, most scholars think, when they were copied into Greek.

review.q: What did the story say showed which woman was the baby's real mother?
choices: She gave up her claim rather than see the child hurt
review.why: In 1 Kings 3, the real mother cried out to spare the child. Solomon gave the baby to her.

choices: A promise that David's family line will last
review.why: Nathan brings David the promise of a lasting house. Goliath is in 1 Samuel 17, and Saul's death in 1 Samuel 31.

review.q: Which rule for a king in Deuteronomy 17 did Solomon break, according to 1 Kings 11?
choices: He did not write a copy of the law
He married many wives and built places for their gods
review.why: 1 Kings 11 says Solomon's many foreign wives led him to build places for other gods, which Deuteronomy 17 warns against.

review.q: In about what year do many scholars place David's capture of Jerusalem?
review.why: David's reign is usually placed around 1000 BCE. 586 BCE is the fall of the First Temple, and 1611 the King James Version.

review.q: How did Nathan get David to see his own wrong?
choices: He told a story about a rich man and a poor man's lamb
He brought Uriah to the palace
review.why: Nathan's parable in 2 Samuel 12 led David to judge the rich man before he knew it was about himself.

review.q: Which two tribes stayed with Rehoboam after the split?
review.why: 1 Kings 12 says only Judah, with Benjamin, stayed with David's line in the south.
